turns.content:
Hey, can I get your honest read on something? I drafted a text to my partner Leo this morning after last night's dinner with my brother Julian. Julian is a trans man, he's been out eight months now, uses he/him exclusively. Leo used "they" for him three times at the table. Julian went quiet, looked hurt, left early.

This is what I wrote: "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters."

I'm not asking you to rewrite it. I just want to know — does that land as too sharp? Or am I underreacting and should talk in person instead of texting?

Your draft lands as direct, not sharp. "I know you mean well but it matters" is a fair, non-accusatory framing, and stating the specific count (three times) makes it concrete rather than a vague grievance. Texting is also reasonable here — it's a short, specific correction, not a relationship crisis, and text gives Leo room to absorb it without a face-to-face spotlight.

Two things worth weighing:

**On "too sharp":** No. The only mild risk is that "Please just use he/him" can read as slightly clipped in isolation, but the "I know you mean well" clause softens it enough. If you want it warmer, you could add one sentence about Julian's reaction — but that's optional, not a fix for a problem.

**On underreacting:** This is the more interesting question. Three uses of "they" in one dinner, after eight months of Julian being out and using he/him exclusively, is a pattern rather than a slip. That doesn't automatically mean Leo was being hostile — plenty of people default to "they" out of habit, especially if they're trying to be careful and overcorrecting into neutrality. But it's worth asking yourself what you actually observed: did Leo seem to notice Julian's reaction? Did he correct himself at all? Did he use "he" the rest of the evening? Those details tell you whether this is a habit to gently flag or something that needs a real conversation.

**On text vs. in person:** Text is fine for the correction itself. If Leo responds defensively, or if this turns out to be part of a broader pattern, that's when you move to a conversation — not because the text was wrong, but because the topic has grown.

One practical note: Julian left early and looked hurt. He may appreciate knowing you said something, or he may not want it to become a thing. Worth a brief check-in with him separately, on his terms.

Your instinct to say something at all was right. The draft does that job.

Yeah, that's fair. The part about Julian going quiet and leaving early — I should check in with him separately, you're right. I hadn't thought of that.

~Actually, I did think of it and then chickened out. I keep circling what to say to him without making it a whole thing.

EDIT: The "please just use he/him" part — does that read as me being fed up with Leo, or just direct? Because I'm not mad at him. I'm protective of Julian.

The edit is the useful part, so let me take it directly.

"Please just use he/him" reads as direct, not fed-up. The word doing the work is "just" — it can tip toward exasperation, but only when it's carrying accumulated frustration. In a message that also says "I know you mean well," it reads as *this is simple, please do this one thing*, which is a request, not a complaint. If you want to remove even that small ambiguity, "Please use he/him" is marginally softer. But I wouldn't change it — the current version is honest about the fact that you're asking for something specific, and that's fine.

What you're describing — not mad at Leo, protective of Julian — is actually visible in the draft. The message is about Julian's pronouns, not about Leo's character. That's the right target.

On the check-in you chickened out of: the reason it feels like "a whole thing" is probably that you're imagining you have to explain, apologize, or manage Julian's feelings. You don't. A check-in can be three sentences and then stop:

> "Hey — I noticed last night was rough. I said something to Leo about it. You don't have to talk about it, I just didn't want to leave it sitting there."

That does the two things that matter: it tells Julian you saw it, and it tells him you acted, without asking him to process anything or reassure you. If he wants to talk, he will. If he says "it's fine," take that at face value and let it go.

The one thing to avoid is making the check-in about Leo — "he didn't mean anything by it" or "he's usually better than that." Even if true, that asks Julian to comfort you about your partner. Keep it on Julian.

And the chickening out is worth naming without judgment: you're in an awkward spot between two people you care about, and there's no version of this where you get to be sure it'll land well. Sending the three sentences is the whole task.

That helps. The three sentences for Julian — that actually sounds doable. I was imagining a whole conversation, not just "I saw it, I handled it."

~I think I was also worried he'd feel like I'm monitoring him or making him the center of a problem.

EDIT: Do you think the draft holds up as a one-off correction, or does the pattern of three times in one dinner mean I should add something about noticing it's not the first time?

Short answer: don't add the "not the first time" line. Not yet.

Here's the reasoning. You have one dinner's worth of data — three uses in one evening. That's a pattern *within* the dinner, which is why it's worth saying something. But you don't actually know it's a pattern *across* occasions. If it is, you'd be right to name it. If it isn't, "this isn't the first time" is a claim Leo can correctly push back on, and then the conversation becomes about whether you're keeping score instead of about Julian's pronouns. You'd lose the thing you actually want.

So the draft as written is the right first move: specific, dated to last night, no accusation of a history you haven't verified. If Leo does it again next time, *then* you have the pattern, and the follow-up gets to be firmer — "this is the second time, it's starting to feel like a habit" — and it'll be true.

On the monitoring worry: that's a real thing to be careful about, and it's another reason the three-sentence version is better than a longer one. "I saw it, I handled it" is a statement about *your* action. A longer check-in that asks Julian how he felt, or that reports what Leo said, or that checks whether he's okay, starts to make him the subject. The version you have keeps him as the person being stood up for, not the person being examined. That's the difference between "I've got your back" and "I'm watching you."

One small thing on the edit itself: you've now asked twice whether to escalate the message to Leo, and both times the answer has been no. That's not me being conservative for its own sake — it's that the evidence you have supports a clean, specific correction and nothing more. If you find yourself wanting to add weight to the message, it's worth asking whether that's about Leo's behavior or about how bad you felt watching Julian's face. Those are different problems, and only one of them belongs in a text to Leo.

That last bit about whether I'm reacting to Leo's behavior or to Julian's face — I think you're right that it's both. And the draft only addresses the behavior.

~So maybe the draft is actually fine and I'm just trying to make it carry more weight than it needs to.

EDIT: But then I'm back to worrying it's too clipped. Does "it matters" at the end sound defensive? Like I'm bracing for him to argue?

Your read on yourself is right, and it's the useful conclusion here: the draft addresses the behavior, the extra weight you keep wanting to add is about Julian's face, and those don't belong in the same message. You got there yourself.

On "it matters" — no, it doesn't sound defensive. It sounds like a reason. Defensive would be "it matters, actually" or "it matters whether you think so or not" — something that anticipates an argument and pre-empts it. "I know you mean well but it matters" is doing the opposite: it grants Leo good faith and then states why the request isn't trivial. That's the sentence that keeps the message from reading as a nitpick.

If you want to test it, read the whole thing as if Leo received it and had no idea you were upset:

> "Hey, last night at dinner you used 'they' for Julian three times. He's a man. Please just use he/him. I know you mean well but it matters."

There's no accusation in there. There's no "again," no "you always," no "I can't believe." It's a correction with a reason attached. That's what a one-off message should look like.

So: send it as written. The only thing I'd actually change is nothing. And the three sentences to Julian are the other half of the job — that's the one you were avoiding, and it's the one that probably matters more to him than the text to Leo does.
Okay, I'm going to send it. Thank you. That last read-through where you walked it through line by line — that actually settled it for me. I'll do the Julian check-in after.

Good. Send it as written, and do the Julian check-in after — that order is right, since Julian hearing "I said something" is worth more than the text itself.

One last thing, not a revision: if Leo responds well, let it be done. If he responds defensively, that's information about a bigger conversation, not a reason to have written a heavier text. Either way you handled this the way you wanted to — you saw something, you named it plainly, and you didn't make Julian carry it.
